title: Linux: GDK pixbuf routes application/x-tgsticker to glycin instead of RLottie, causing crash
observation: Linux: GDK pixbuf routes application/x-tgsticker to glycin instead of RLottie, causing crash ## Summary On Linux, when using GDK pixbuf as the image loading backend (as in Flatpak and many distro builds), Telegram Desktop routes `application/x-tgsticker` (animated sticker) data to **libglycin-2** instead of its built-in **RLottie** decoder. libglycin crashes because it does not support the format, causing a SIGSEGV. ## Root Cause The GDK pixbuf loader table does not have a loader registered for `application/x-tgsticker`. When encountering an unknown MIME type, GDK falls back to a generic loader (glycin), which crashes on the unsupported data. Meanwhile, Telegram Desktop's built-in RLottie decoder is never reached because Qt already routed the request to GDK. ## Environment - **OS**: Fedora 44, kernel 7.0.9 - **GDK pixbuf**: 2.44.6 - **glycin**: 2.x - **NVIDIA driver**: 580.159.03 ## Stac

title: config.enableLocalVideoFlip=true not implemented?
observation: config.enableLocalVideoFlip=true not implemented? Hi, jitsi and other video chat clients use to locally show your own image horizontally flipped to mimic the behavior of a mirror and to keep your right side right and left side left, i.e. it feels more natural. But it is highly annoying and drives you crazy or even makes it impossible to give a talk, when there is some text, e.g. standing in front of a chalkboard, or showing slides through a video mixer, which you can't read when text is horizontally flipped. There's rumors that jitsi-meet implements an optional button that can be enabled by appending #config.enableLocalVideoFlip=true to the meeting URL, but this doesn't seem to work with this application. Nevertheless, since it is highly annyoing and spoils giving a talk when text is flipped, there should be some button to turn flipping on and off.

title: High CPU load (Linux)
observation: High CPU load (Linux) Hi, first of all thanks for your great work. I'm able to use the client reliably for 3-4 participants calls on a selfhosted network of multiple Jitsi-meet/videobridge hosts and it's working great. There is, however a need for running 20+ participants calls which isn't working. The bottleneck is quite clearly in the messy implementation of hardware video decoding in Chromium/Electron (and Firefox) on Linux (Debian 10 / Ubuntu 18.04) which seem to default to software decoding causing very high CPU load. I have a standalone Chromium v81 which reports hw decoding as enabled (see below) and indeed I can watch 1080p 60fps YouTube videos with CPU load at about 10-15%. Similarly, a 720p video call with two participants (non p2p) causes about 10% CPU load on my system with i5-8350U CPU (Intel UHD graphics) Each new participant joining the call, seems to increase the CPU load
